title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 819–820 (Night 176, continuing nights-175), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 176 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. In the old tower where his father has shut him up, the prince, having prayed the sunset and night prayers, sits on his couch and recites from the Qurʾān — al-Baqara, Āl ʿImrān, Yā Sīn, al-Raḥmān, Tabāraka al-Mulk, al-Ikhlāṣ and the two suras of refuge — then closes with a prayer, seeks God's protection and lies down on a mattress of satin stuffed with Iraqi silk, a pillow of ostrich down beneath his head. He undresses, sleeps in a fine shirt with a blue Marw kerchief on his head, like the full moon on its fourteenth night, the lantern lit at his feet and the candle above his head, knowing nothing of what lies hidden for him. For the tower and its hall had stood deserted for years, and in the hall was an old Roman well inhabited by a jinniya of the progeny of Iblīs, Maymūna, daughter of al-Dimiryāṭ, one of the famous kings of the jinn — and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-sixth night,
sentences.n: The formula as before, with al-sādisa, “the sixth”, feminine to agree with layla.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ ابْنَ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ لَمَّا صَلَّى الْمَغْرِبَ وَالْعِشَاءَ جَلَسَ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ يَقْرَأُ الْقُرْآنَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni ibna al-maliki Shahramāna lammā ṣallā al-maghriba wa-al-ʿishāʾa jalasa ʿalā al-sarīri yaqraʾu al-qurʾāna
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, (the) son of the-king Shahramān, when he-prayed the-sunset and the-nightfall, sat on the-bed reciting the-Qurʾān.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān, son of King Shahramān, had prayed the sunset and night prayers, he sat on the bed reciting the Qurʾān.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up where the last night stopped, with the prince at his evening prayers. lammā … jalasa, “when … he sat”: lammā with the perfect, answered by a second perfect. yaqraʾu, “reciting”, an imperfect standing as a circumstantial clause after jalasa, “he sat (and was) reciting”. qaraʾa is “to read” and, of the Qurʾān, “to recite”. The shadda of صلّى and the hamza and madda of يقرأ and القرآن are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَرَأَ الْبَقَرَةَ وَآلَ عِمْرَانَ وَيَاسِينَ وَالرَّحْمٰنَ وَتَبَارَكَ الْمُلْكَ وَالْإِخْلَاصَ وَالْمُعَوِّذَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qaraʾa al-Baqarata wa-Āla ʿImrāna wa-Yāsīna wa-al-Raḥmāna wa-Tabāraka al-Mulka wa-al-Ikhlāṣa wa-al-Muʿawwidhatayni
sentences.l: And-he-recited the-Cow and-(the)-Family (of) ʿImrān and-Yā-Sīn and-the-Merciful and-Blessed-is the-Kingship and-the-Sincerity and-the-Two-Refuge-Givers.
sentences.i: He recited al-Baqara, Āl ʿImrān, Yā Sīn, al-Raḥmān, Tabāraka al-Mulk, al-Ikhlāṣ and the two suras of refuge.
sentences.n: Suras of the Qurʾān, each named, as usual, by a word from it: al-Baqara, “the Cow” (sura 2), and Āl ʿImrān, “the Family of ʿImrān” (3), two of the longest; Yā Sīn (36), named from the two letters that open it, here spelt out as a word; al-Raḥmān, “the Merciful” (55), written, as in the Qurʾān, without the long alif, which the small upright alif supplies; Tabāraka al-Mulk (67), usually called simply al-Mulk, “the Kingship”, here named by its first word tabāraka, “blessed is (He)”, and al-mulk from the same verse (tabāraka alladhī bi-yadihi al-mulku, “blessed is He in whose hand is the kingship”), the two run together as one title; al-Ikhlāṣ, “Sincere Faith” (112); and al-Muʿawwidhatān, “the two (suras) that give refuge”, that is, that protect (113 and 114), which open “Say: I seek refuge with the Lord…”, in the accusative dual al-muʿawwidhatayni. Al-Mulk, al-Ikhlāṣ and the two refuge suras are traditionally recited before sleep for protection, which is the point here. The titles are given the accusative as objects of qaraʾa. The shadda of المعوّذتين and the hamza of فقرأ and the madda of وآل are printed.

sentences.i: He closed with a prayer of supplication, fortified himself, and took refuge in God,
sentences.n: khatama bi-, “to close with, end with”: bi- marks what he ends on. al-duʿāʾ is a personal prayer of request, as against the set ṣalāt. taḥaṣṣana, Form V of ḥaṣuna, “to be fortified”, is “to make oneself safe”, here by the protective suras and prayers just recited. istaʿādha bi-, Form X, “to seek refuge with”, the verb of the two refuge suras: bi- marks the one in whom refuge is sought. The shadda of تحصّن is printed.

sentences.t: وَنَامَ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ فَوْقَ طَرَّاحَةٍ مِنَ الْأَطْلَسِ الْمَعْدِنِيِّ لَهَا وَجْهَانِ وَهِيَ مَحْشُوَّةٌ بِالْخَزِّ الْعِرَاقِيِّ
sentences.tr: wa-nāma ʿalā al-sarīri fawqa ṭarrāḥatin mina al-aṭlasi al-maʿdiniyyi lahā wajhāni wa-hiya maḥshuwwatun bi-al-khazzi al-ʿirāqiyyi
sentences.l: and-slept on the-bed, above a-mattress of the-satin the-mineral, to-it (were) two-faces, and-it (was) stuffed with-the-silk the-Iraqi.
sentences.i: and lay down to sleep on the bed, upon a mattress of metallic satin, faced on both sides and stuffed with Iraqi silk.
sentences.n: ṭarrāḥa, “mattress, thin quilt laid on a couch”, from ṭaraḥa, “to throw down, spread”. aṭlas is a smooth, glossy satin. al-aṭlas al-maʿdinī, literally “mineral satin”: maʿdinī is “of the mine, metallic”, and the phrase seems to name a satin shot with metal thread, or with a metallic sheen; the precise stuff is not certain. lahā wajhāni, “to it two faces”: the satin is on both sides, it can be turned. khazz is a fabric of silk, or silk mixed with wool. The shaddas of طرّاحة, محشوّة and الخزّ are printed.

sentences.t: وَتَحْتَ رَأْسِهِ مِخَدَّةٌ مَحْشُوَّةٌ بِرِيشِ النَّعَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-taḥta raʾsihi mikhaddatun maḥshuwwatun bi-rīshi al-naʿāmi
sentences.l: And-under his-head (was) a-pillow stuffed with-(the)-feathers (of) the-ostriches.
sentences.i: Under his head was a pillow stuffed with ostrich feathers.
sentences.n: A nominal sentence with the place put first: taḥta raʾsihi, “under his head”, then the indefinite subject mikhadda, “pillow”, from khadd, “cheek”, the thing one lays the cheek on. naʿām is the collective, “ostriches”. The print marks the shadda of مخدّة but not of the second محشوة, where it is supplied; the hamza of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: وَحِينَ أَرَادَ النَّوْمَ تَجَرَّدَ مِنْ ثِيَابِهِ وَخَلَعَ لِبَاسَهُ وَنَامَ فِي قَمِيصٍ مُشَمَّعٍ رَفِيعٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥīna arāda al-nawma tajarrada min thiyābihi wa-khalaʿa libāsahu wa-nāma fī qamīṣin mushammaʿin rafīʿin
sentences.l: And-when he-wanted the-sleep, he-stripped from his-clothes, and-took-off his-drawers, and-slept in a-shirt waxed fine.
sentences.i: When he was ready to sleep he stripped off his clothes, took off his drawers, and slept in a fine shirt of waxed cloth.
sentences.n: ḥīna, “at the time when”, an accusative of time used as a conjunction. tajarrada min, Form V, “to strip oneself of”: min marks what is taken off; its shadda is printed. libās, “clothing”, is in this text usually the drawers worn under the outer clothes, which is how it is taken here after thiyāb, “clothes”. mushammaʿ is “waxed, treated with wax”, from shamʿ, “wax”; a waxed shirt is an odd thing to sleep in, and the word may name a glazed or lustrous cloth; it is translated literally, with that doubt. rafīʿ, “fine, thin”, of cloth.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ مِقْنَعٌ مَرْوَزِيٌّ أَزْرَقُ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna ʿalā raʾsihi miqnaʿun marwaziyyun azraqu
sentences.l: And-was on his-head a-head-cloth Marwazī blue.
sentences.i: On his head was a blue head-cloth of Marw.
sentences.n: Here kāna stands first with its subject miqnaʿ, “head-cloth, veil”, in the nominative, and the place ʿalā raʾsihi before it. marwazī, “of Marw”, is the adjective from Marw (Merv) in Khurasan, a city famous for fine fabrics, formed irregularly with a z. azraq, “blue”, is a diptote, so azraqu has no tanwīn. The hamza of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ تِلْكَ السَّاعَةَ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ كَأَنَّهُ الْبَدْرُ إِذَا بَدَرَ لَيْلَةَ أَرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra Qamaru al-Zamāni tilka al-sāʿata fī hādhihi al-laylati ka-annahu al-badru idhā badara laylata arbaʿata ʿashara
sentences.l: And-became Qamar al-Zamān that the-hour in this the-night as-if-he (were) the-full-moon when it-rises-full (on the) night (of) four-ten.
sentences.i: And Qamar al-Zamān, at that hour on this night, was like the full moon when it rises full on the fourteenth night.
sentences.n: ṣāra, “became”, with its predicate a clause, ka-annahu …, “as if he were …”. The print spells كانه with a bare alif and no hamza, as it often does; it is read ka-annahu. al-badru idhā badara plays on the noun and the verb: badr is the full moon, and badara, “to come on suddenly”, is said of the moon rising full. laylata arbaʿata ʿashara, “the night of fourteen”, is the night of the full moon, the fourteenth of the lunar month; the date is put as a bare number in construct, “fourteen”, in the masculine form, where Classical, counting nights (feminine), would say laylata arbaʿa ʿashrata, or with the ordinal laylata al-rābiʿata ʿashrata. The prince is named for the moon: Qamar al-Zamān, “Moon of the Age”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَغَطَّى بِمُلَاءَةٍ مِنْ حَرِيرٍ وَنَامَ وَالْفَانُوسُ مَوْقُودٌ تَحْتَ رِجْلَيْهِ وَالشَّمْعَةُ مَوْقُودَةٌ فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma taghaṭṭā bi-mulāʾatin min ḥarīrin wa-nāma wa-al-fānūsu mawqūdun taḥta rijlayhi wa-al-shamʿatu mawqūdatun fawqa raʾsihi
sentences.l: Then he-covered-himself with-a-sheet of silk, and-slept, and-the-lantern (was) lit below his-two-feet, and-the-candle lit above his-head.
sentences.i: Then he covered himself with a sheet of silk and slept, while the lantern stayed lit below his feet and the candle above his head.
sentences.n: taghaṭṭā bi-, Form V, “to cover oneself with”: bi- marks the covering; its shadda is printed, as is the hamza of ملاءة. mulāʾa, “sheet, wrap”. wa-al-fānūsu …, a circumstantial clause introduced by wa-, “(while) the lantern …”. mawqūd, “lit”, the passive participle of waqada, “to burn”, where Classical prefers mūqad, from Form IV awqada; mawqūd is the common later form. taḥta rijlayhi … fawqa raʾsihi, “below his feet … above his head”, balance each other; the lantern and candle are those the servant lit for him in the last night.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ نَائِمًا إِلَى ثُلُثِ اللَّيْلِ الْأَوَّلِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal nāʾiman ilā thuluthi al-layli al-awwali
sentences.l: And-not he-ceased sleeping until (the) third (of) the-night the-first.
sentences.i: He went on sleeping through the first third of the night,
sentences.n: lam yazal, “he did not cease”, with the predicate nāʾiman, “sleeping”, in the accusative: “he went on sleeping”. thuluth al-layl al-awwal, “the first third of the night”: al-awwal agrees with thuluth, not with layl. The ئ of نائما is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ مَا خُبِئَ لَهُ فِى الْغَيْبِ وَمَا قَدَّرَهُ عَلَيْهِ عَلَّامُ الْغَيْبِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yaʿlam mā khubiʾa lahu fī al-ghaybi wa-mā qaddarahu ʿalayhi ʿallāmu al-ghaybi
sentences.l: and-not he-knew what was-hidden for-him in the-unseen, and-what decreed-it upon-him (the) Knower (of) the-unseen.
sentences.i: and did not know what lay hidden for him in the unseen, nor what the Knower of the unseen had decreed for him.
sentences.n: The sentence rhymes on itself, al-ghayb / al-ghayb. khubiʾa, passive of khabaʾa, “to hide, store away”. al-ghayb, “the unseen, the hidden”, what is beyond human knowledge, the future above all. qaddara ʿalā, “to decree for, ordain against”: ʿalā marks the one it falls on. ʿallām, “all-knowing”, an intensive form; ʿallāmu al-ghaybi (or al-ghuyūbi) is an epithet of God. The print writes في as فى; the hamza of خبئ and the shaddas of قدّره and علّام are printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ بِالْأَمْرِ الْمُقَدَّرِ وَالْقَضَاءِ الْمُتَحَتِّمِ أَنَّ هٰذَا الْبُرْجَ وَهٰذِهِ الْقَاعَةَ كَانَا عَتِيقَيْنِ مَهْجُورَيْنِ مِنْ مُدَّةِ سِنِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna bi-al-amri al-muqaddari wa-al-qaḍāʾi al-mutaḥattimi anna hādhā al-burja wa-hādhihi al-qāʿata kānā ʿatīqayni mahjūrayni min muddati sinīna
sentences.l: And-it-was, by-the-matter the-decreed and-the-judgement the-inescapable, that this the-tower and-this the-hall were-both old abandoned since (a) period (of) years.
sentences.i: Now, by the matter decreed and the judgement that cannot be escaped, this tower and this hall had stood old and deserted for years.
sentences.n: wa-kāna … anna, “and it was … that”: kāna has the whole anna clause as its subject, and bi- marks what brought it about, “by the decree”. al-qaḍāʾ, “judgement”, God's fixed decision; al-mutaḥattim, “made binding, inevitable”, Form V from ḥatm. The shadda of المقدّر is printed. kānā, the dual, for tower and hall together, with the dual predicates ʿatīqayni mahjūrayni in the accusative. This is the old tower, with its ruined hall, in which the prince was shut up in Night 174. min muddati sinīna, “since a period of years”: min of the starting point, “for years past”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ فِي تِلْكَ الْقَاعَةِ بِئْرٌ رُومَانِيٌّ مَعْمُورَةٌ بِجِنِّيَّةٍ سَاكِنَةٍ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kānat fī tilka al-qāʿati biʾrun rūmāniyyun maʿmūratun bi-jinniyyatin sākinatin fīhā
sentences.l: And-was in that the-hall a-well Roman inhabited by-a-jinniya dwelling in-it.
sentences.i: In that hall there was a Roman well, inhabited by a jinniya who lived in it.
sentences.n: biʾr, “well”, is feminine, so kānat and maʿmūra, “inhabited, peopled”, are feminine; but rūmānī, “Roman”, between them, is masculine, a loose agreement the text allows itself and kept as printed. rūmānī is “Roman”, that is, old, of the ancient builders; the plain word for “Roman, Byzantine” is rūmī. maʿmūra bi-, “peopled with”: bi- marks who lives there. jinniyya is a female jinn. The hamza of بئر and the shadda of جنّية are printed.

sentences.t: وَهِيَ مِنْ ذُرِّيَّةِ إِبْلِيسَ اللَّعِينِ وَاسْمُهَا مَيْمُونَةُ ابْنَةُ الدِّ مِرْيَاطِ أَحَدِ مُلُوكِ الْجَانِّ الْمَشْهُورِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-hiya min dhurriyyati Iblīsa al-laʿīni wa-ismuhā Maymūnatu ibnatu al-Di miryāṭi aḥadi mulūki al-jānni al-mashhūrīna
sentences.l: And-she (was) of (the) offspring (of) Iblīs the-accursed, and-her-name (was) Maymūna, daughter (of) al-Dimiryāṭ, one (of the) kings (of) the-jinn the-famous.
sentences.i: She was descended from Iblīs the accursed, and her name was Maymūna, daughter of al-Dimiryāṭ, one of the famous kings of the jinn.
sentences.n: Her lineage is given in full: of the dhurriyya, “offspring, progeny”, of Iblīs, the Devil, and daughter of a named jinn king. The print sets her father's name as two words, الد مرياط; it is one name, al-Dimiryāṭ, and the split is kept as printed. The vocalisation of so rare a name is uncertain. aḥadi, “one of”, is in the genitive in apposition to al-Dimiryāṭ, and al-mashhūrīna, “the famous”, goes with mulūk, “kings”. Maymūna, “the fortunate”, is an ordinary woman's name. The shadda of ذرّية is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ مِنَ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat mina al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The formula as before, except that here the print has min, “from”, where everywhere else it has ʿan; min reads well enough, “fell silent from”, and is kept. As always, the morning overtakes Shahrazād, and the rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥu / al-mubāḥi.
